<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and used the pressure round effectively. B's rebuttal 1 and OS-level certificate revocation argument (B4.1) was the strongest single move of the debate, forcing A to concede that payment control isn't the exclusive source of enforcement power. But A adapted by narrowing to a sharper, more concrete fallback: even if the OS can eventually disable a malicious app, chargebacks and cross-border processor licensing are slow while financial theft is instant, so "certificate revocation cannot un-steal money." B's closing answer to this ("a tuning problem for baseline standards to solve") never specified a mechanism for matching in-store speed, leaving A's timing gap as the one clearly live, unresolved point at the end of the debate. A's closing crystallized this into a memorable, weighted comparison (speculative savings vs. certain harm to the least protected users) that B's rent-extraction reframing did not squarely answer. B's opening being clipped is a minor execution cost. The result is close, but A ends the exchange holding the one major unresolved thread.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's OS-certificate-revocation mechanism (B4.1) was the most theoretically decisive move, separating enforcement power from payment control; A's counter-narrowing to "certificate revocation cannot un-steal money" (A4.4/A5.2) was the most damaging comeback, since B's closing never rebutted the months-vs-minutes timing gap it exposed.</best_rebuttal>
